name: Aqualyx

lead: Aqualyx is a CE-marked injectable made from deoxycholic acid, a bile acid that dissolves fat cell membranes. In Europe it is sold to trained practitioners to reduce small fat pockets such as under the chin, and forum users discuss it for slimming the cheeks, jaw and neck to get a leaner, more defined lower face.

Deoxycholate acts like a detergent on fat cell membranes, the cells break open and the body clears the debris, with inflammation and later fibrosis described in the treated area. Published evidence is limited to small studies and case reports, and no published trial has tested facial hollowing as described in forums. The related drug Kybella is the US-approved deoxycholic acid product for submental fat.

paras: Practitioners inject it into the targeted fat pocket, sometimes with ultrasound guidance, over a series of sessions. Forum users report using it on the lower face, and claims of permanence are anecdotal.

Reported effects are swelling, bruising and pain, and a published case described chronic infection and nodule formation after a deoxycholate injection. Aqualyx is not FDA-approved, counterfeits have been discussed in forums, the manufacturer sells only to trained professionals and self-injection is outside labelled use.

angle.text: Aqualyx is a deoxycholate injectable sold in Europe to dissolve localized fat, and forum users discuss it for slimming the cheeks, jaw and neck. It breaks down fat cells in the treated area so the lower face looks leaner. Facial use goes beyond published studies, and claims of permanence are anecdotal.

lead: Aqualyx is a gel-like aqueous solution of sodium deoxycholate, developed in Italy by Professor Pasquale Motolese and commercially available since 2009, marketed by Marllor and sold to doctors and nurses trained in intralipotherapy [1][2]. It is CE-marked in the European Union and used to dissolve small pockets of subcutaneous fat [2][1]. A 2022 case report describes it as a deoxycholate solution mixed with saline and buffering compounds [1].

In looksmaxxing communities it is used or discussed as a way to slim the lower face: thinning the submental area under the chin to sharpen the jawline and neck angle, and reducing cheek or buccal fat for a more defined, hollowed mid-face. The chain is direct: fat cells in the treated area are broken down, the area becomes leaner, and the underlying bone and muscle contours read more clearly.

Deoxycholic acid is a naturally occurring bile acid; the US FDA approved a different deoxycholic acid product, Kybella, for submental fat in 2015 [3][4]. Aqualyx has no FDA approval [2]. Published studies of Aqualyx and similar deoxycholate intralipotherapy cover body fat deposits, lipomas and a rare fat disorder; no published trial has evaluated it for facial slimming [5][6][7][8][9].

paras: Aqualyx is a branded injectable whose active ingredient is sodium deoxycholate, a salt of a bile acid the body normally uses to emulsify dietary fat. It is supplied as a clear aqueous gel-like solution that practitioners place into subcutaneous fat with fine needles, a method that the European aesthetic-medicine literature calls intralipotherapy [1][7]. The product is positioned as an alternative to liposuction for small, localized deposits: under the chin, on the abdomen and flanks, the inner knees and similar areas [2][10][7].

Intralipotherapy belongs to a wider family of techniques known as injection lipolysis, in which drug mixtures are injected to destroy fat cells. Earlier mixtures combined phosphatidylcholine with deoxycholate (PCDC), and the best-known preparation, Lipostabil, was a German-approved intravenous product for other conditions whose off-label cosmetic use started the practice [11]. Aqualyx and the US drug Kybella use deoxycholate alone, without phosphatidylcholine [3][11].

Per Grokipedia, intended targets are small, pinchable pockets of fat such as the chin, abdomen, flanks and thighs [2]. Practitioner-led treatment is described as multiple sessions spaced weeks apart [2]. A 2016 review of intralipotherapy, a term used mainly in European aesthetic medicine for injecting substances that lyse fat cells directly into adipose tissue through a long needle, reported that 3,080 European physicians were trained in the technique between 2010 and 2014 and that roughly 152,500 patients were treated [7].

sections.h: How it is used for the face
paras: Within appearance communities, the main appeal is facial slimming. The chin and hyoid area is treated to sharpen the line between jaw and neck; the lower cheek or jowl region is treated by users who want a leaner mid-face and more visible cheekbone and jaw contours. Posters on looksmax.org describe sessions spaced weeks apart, with visible swelling in the days after each injection, and compare their results with photographs of treated areas [10][12].

Forum guides describe do-it-yourself preparation, marking and injection for the neck area. This wiki does not reproduce those instructions. The reference point most posters use is the US-approved Kybella treatment grid for the submental area [3][4]. Clinic-based treatment, where the product is sold to trained doctors and nurses, is the labelled route in Europe [1].

Deoxycholic acid disrupts the lipid membranes of fat cells, releasing their contents and prompting an inflammatory response in which macrophages clear debris, followed by fibrosis [2]. A 2018 study describes the effect as emulsification of phospholipids and solubilisation of cell membranes, producing fat necrosis [6]. The US-approved relative, Kybella, is described by Wikipedia as destroying submental fat cells that the body then metabolises over several months [3].

Because the target is cell membranes, the effect is not specific to one tissue type. Deoxycholate is described as a cytolytic agent that can also affect skin and muscle cells if it spreads beyond the fat layer, which is why reviews emphasise needle depth, spacing and anatomical knowledge [7]. The Kybella label tells clinicians to stay within the submental target area and away from a band below the jaw edge, because the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve runs nearby [4].

A 2019 evaluation study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology treated 17 lipomas with ultrasound-guided Aqualyx injections, up to three per lesion; all responded, 70.59 percent were completely removed and the rest were significantly reduced [5]. A 2018 multicentre observational study (February to October 2017) of a 1.25 percent sodium deoxycholate solution treated 221 patients with localised fat in several areas at 6-week intervals until a result was reached, with outcomes judged from photographs and patient satisfaction forms [6]. The 2016 intralipotherapy review reported effectiveness in an average of 76.7 percent of cases across zones, varying with area and patient [7]. A 2021 study of seven women treated twice, four weeks apart, for fat on the inner knees under ultrasound guidance found reduced knee circumference and subcutaneous tissue in 71.42 percent of patients [8]. A report of two patients with Madelung's disease treated with serial phosphatidylcholine/deoxycholate injections found an average 42.5 percent size reduction and about a 33 percent recurrence rate over five years [9].

The approved relative has a larger trial record. Per its US label, two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in adults with moderate to severe submental fat reported that at 12 weeks after the final session, 13.4 and 18.6 percent of Kybella-treated participants reached a two-grade improvement on a composite scale, against under 0.1 and 3.0 percent with placebo; a one-grade improvement was seen in 70.0 and 66.5 percent, against 18.6 and 22.2 percent. In an MRI subset, 43 percent of treated participants had at least a 10 percent reduction in submental fat volume versus 5 percent with placebo [4]. These results concern Kybella, not Aqualyx.
A 2022 case report documented chronic infection and nodule formation after deoxycholate injection [1]. No published studies were found on Aqualyx for facial hollowing or buccal fat reduction.

Grokipedia lists swelling, bruising and discomfort as common, with infection and nodules reported in some cases [2]. A 2022 case report described chronic infection and nodule formation after injection of an advertised deoxycholate product, noting Aqualyx is sold only to trained clinicians [1]. The facial region contains small nerves and vessels, and reviews of intralipotherapy describe the technique, protocol and post-treatment management as needed to minimise adverse events [7].

For Kybella, the US label records temporary asymmetric smile or facial muscle weakness from marginal mandibular nerve injury in trials, all resolving without treatment (1 to 298 days, median 44), and difficulty swallowing that resolved in 1 to 81 days (median 3); the label advises avoiding use in people with current or prior dysphagia [4]. Wikipedia notes that earlier unapproved lipodissolve products drew an FDA warning-letter action in April 2010 after reports of scarring, skin deformation and painful knots, and that three US plastic-surgery and dermatologic-surgery societies have cautioned against such injections [11].

In Europe the product sits within aesthetic-medicine practice, where it is administered by trained practitioners [1][7]. On looksmax.org, threads discuss price, authenticity, results photographs and swelling after sessions, and users have posted about injecting themselves; the wiki does not reproduce dosing or technique details [10][12]. Threads include warnings about counterfeit products and disputes about whether the outcome is permanent.

In the European Union the product is CE-marked and, per the 2022 case report, sold only to doctors and nurses trained in the technique [1]. In the United States Aqualyx is not FDA-approved [2]; the approved deoxycholic acid product is Kybella (Belkyra elsewhere), prescription-only in the US, Australia and the EU, and generic deoxycholic acid has been available in the US since April 2021 [3][4]. The UK's regulator has previously warned that injection-lipolysis drugs were being unlawfully advertised as cosmetic fat reducers, and the FDA issued warning letters over unapproved lipodissolve products in 2010 [11].

Related approaches to a leaner lower face include Kybella treatment by a licensed provider [3][4], buccal fat removal surgery, liposuction of the neck and jowls, and non-surgical body-fat reduction, which forum users often discuss alongside Aqualyx. Phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate mixtures and other lipolysis injectables are covered under injection lipolysis [11].

lore.intro: Aqualyx is discussed on looksmax.org as a cheaper route to a leaner face, with threads on sourcing, authenticity, swelling and results [10][12].

claims.claim: Aqualyx gives a permanent hollow-cheek look.
Self-injected or imported product is equivalent to clinic treatment.
Swelling after a session is temporary and passes within days or weeks.
Aqualyx can reshape the face as precisely as Kybella treats the chin.
Fakes are common, so product origin decides the outcome.

timeline.event: Investigators report that intravenous phosphatidylcholine solutions can clear fat emboli, an early step toward the lipolysis injections that followed [11].
The FDA issues warning letters over unapproved lipodissolve injection products marketed for fat removal [11].
3,080 European physicians trained in intralipotherapy; about 152,500 patients treated [7].
On April 29, FDA approves Kybella, a different deoxycholic acid product, for fat below the chin [3][4].
Multicentre observational study of 1.25% deoxycholate in 221 patients published [6].
Study of ultrasound-guided Aqualyx injection for lipomas published [5].
Case report of chronic infection and nodules after deoxycholate injection [1].
Intralipotherapy review reports 3,080 trained European physicians and about 152,500 patients treated [7].
Generic deoxycholic acid becomes available in the US [3].
